rationale: B wins because it gives the founder three cleaner, more pitchable tensions without A's extra padding. Its "Going's new planner is a Premium-only perk — and most of its 2 million members can't touch it" has a real consumer-value fight inside it, while A's "The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" is a thin identity-arc profile trying to pass as news. B still has an unsupported industry-narrative problem, but its proof asks would get a usable pitch faster.
gaps_in_A: "how Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" is outside the supplied facts; useful as a comparison to verify, not as asserted context.
"The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" is padding. The update gives a former name, not enough rebrand or platform-evolution evidence to carry a profile angle.
"content-first or newsletter-first companies convert free audiences" imports a media/subscription frame the update does not supply and may send the founder to the wrong desk.
"A tech reporter or columnist" in Angle 2 is too broad. The beat should be travel-tech or AI-agent skepticism, not generic tech coverage.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry" is asserted without evidence. That contrarian angle needs current sources before it can carry weight.
"most of its 2 million members can't touch it" muddies the member math. The update says about 2 million free members plus a smaller paid base, not exactly 2 million total members.
"the deal that lands in your inbox" adds behavior not supplied in the update. Stick to the app/fare-alert trigger unless email delivery is confirmed.
"Next step: meanest-editor" is premature. First verify the AI output, $550 methodology, paid-base size, and no-booking rationale; polish the pitch after the facts stop wobbling.
